questions.question: What are endless methods in Ruby?
questions.title: Endless Methods in Ruby
questions.direct_answer: Endless methods (Ruby 3.0+) let you write a one-line method without `end`: `def greet(name) = "Hello, #{name}"`. The `=` replaces the body delimiter; no end needed. They must be a single expression (no multi-line body). Useful for trivial getters/computed values: `def full_name = [first, last].join(' ')`; `def area = @w * @h`. You can't have a body with multiple statements — use a normal def for that. Endless methods still return the expression (implicit return). They reduce visual noise for tiny methods. Note: no arguments needs empty parens `def x() = 1` (or `def x = 1` is allowed in 3.0+). They're a readability feature — use them for one-liners, fall back to def/end for anything with logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know endless methods (Ruby 3.0+) use `=` instead of end and are for one-line expressions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using an endless method for multi-statement logic (they must be a single expression), or expecting `end`.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Endless methods (Ruby 3.0+): `def f(x) = expr` — one-line, no end. For trivial getters/computed values. Must be a single expression.

sections.title: One-Line, No End
sections.content: Endless methods (Ruby 3.0 plus) let you write a one-line method without end: def greet name equals Hello name. The equals replaces the body delimiter; no end needed. They must be a single expression (no multi-line body). Useful for trivial getters and computed values: def full name equals first last join space; def area equals w times h. You can't have a body with multiple statements — use a normal def for that. Endless methods still return the expression (implicit return). They reduce visual noise for tiny methods. Note: no arguments needs empty parens def x parens equals 1 (or def x equals 1 is allowed in 3.0 plus). They're a readability feature — use them for one-liners, fall back to def end for anything with logic.

flowchart LR

sections.title: Endless methods
sections.content:
```ruby
# Ruby 3.0+: endless methods (no `end`)
def greet(name) = "Hello, #{name}"

greet('Ada')          # 'Hello, Ada'

# Single expression; IMPLICIT return (no return keyword needed)
def square(n) = n * n
square(5)            # 25

# Great for trivial getters / computed values:
class Rect
  def initialize(w, h); @w = w; @h = h; end
  def area = @w * @h            # endless getter
  def perimeter = 2 * (@w + @h)
end
r = Rect.new(3, 4)
r.area          # 12
r.perimeter     # 14

# No args: empty parens (or omit in 3.0+)
def x() = 1
def y = 2        # also valid

# CAN'T have multiple statements — use a normal def:
# def bad = a; b; c    # syntax error (use def/end)

# Use for ONE-LINERS; fall back to def/end for logic.
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using an endless method for multi-statement logic (must be single expression).
Adding explicit `return` (not allowed; it's a single expression).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Endless methods (Ruby 3.0+): `def f(x) = expr` — one line, no end.
They must be a single expression; the expression is returned (implicit return).
Great for trivial getters/computed values (def area = @w * @h).
Fall back to def/end for anything with multiple statements or logic.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Endless methods (Ruby 3.0 plus) let you write a one-line method without end: def greet name equals Hello name. The equals replaces the body delimiter; no end needed. They must be a single expression (no multi-line body). Useful for trivial getters and computed values: def full name equals first last join space; def area equals w times h. You can't have a body with multiple statements — use a normal def for that. Endless methods still return the expression (implicit return). They reduce visual noise for tiny methods. Note: no arguments needs empty parens def x parens equals 1 (or def x equals 1 is allowed in 3.0 plus). They're a readability feature — use them for one-liners, fall back to def end for anything with logic. A common mistake is using an endless method for multi-statement logic, since they must be a single expression, and expecting an end, when there is none.
